Hi, thanks for the UUIDs!

I have a question. I found out the hard way that `stringify` doesn't stringify any old length-16 `UInt8Array`. But I believe `v3` and `v5` do accept any such array, for the namespace. The docs for `v5` say

> namespace   |    String | Array[16] Namespace UUID

but looking through your past gh issues I understand you consider "UUID" to mean "valid UUID", so I though I'd ask for clarification. Are `v3` and `v5` meant to accept any `UInt8Array`, whether a UUID or not?
items.title: Q: Clarify meaning of "UUID" (namespace vs stringify)

items.body:
Would you be open to backporting the fix for GHSA-w5hq-g745-h8pq ? it looks like it should cleanly apply to older versions, and I'm personally happy to help as much as possible to reduce the maintainer overhead.

While I know the vulnerability only impacts some versions and most uses in the wild are of UUID v4, this library is very popular and the v8 version in particular is the most downloaded version - in particular, it's used by `webpack-dev-server` via `sockjs` which has not had a new version in a while.

I understand that ideally the surrounding ecosystem should upgrade and I [am working to try make that happen where I can](https://github.com/sockjs/sockjs-node/pull/315), but if you're willing to backport the fix even just to v8 it would make life easier for a lot of people I think

### Before you begin...

- [x] I have searched the existing issues
- [x] My issue title is descriptive and specific to the problem (i.e. search-engine friendly)
- [x] I understand what an "MRE" is, and why providing one is important.  (If not, [read this](https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example))

### MRE and Description

The `validate()` function uses a regex that restricts the variant nibble to `[89ab]` (variant `10x` per RFC 4122). This causes it to reject UUIDs that are structurally     
  valid but have variant bits `110x` (hex `c` or `d`).                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                              
  AWS Cognito generates UUIDv7 user IDs (`sub` claims) that use variant `110x`. These UUIDs are valid and used in production systems, but `validate()` rejects them.          
   
  ### Reproduction                                                                                                                                                            
                  
  ```ts
  import { validate } from "uuid";
                                                                                                                                                                              
  // Example UUID generated by AWS Cognito (UUIDv7, variant 110x)
  const uuid = "c4b824d8-10f1-70e5-cdcf-0c6229f00024";                                                                                                                        
                                                                                                                                                                              
  console.log(validate(uuid)); // false — but this is a valid UUIDv7
  ```                                                                                                                                                                         
                  
  The version nibble is `7` (valid UUIDv7), and the string is a well-formed 8-4-4-4-12 hex UUID. The only reason it fails validation is the variant nibble `c` (`1100`        
  binary), which falls under variant `110x`.
                                                                                                                                                                              
  ### Current regex

  ```
  /^(?:[0-9a-f]{8}-[0-9a-f]{4}-[1-8][0-9a-f]{3}-[89ab][0-9a-f]{3}-[0-9a-f]{12}|...$/i
  ```                                                                                                                                                                         
   
  The `[89ab]` restricts to variant-1 only.                                                                                                                                   
                  
  ### Expected behavior                                                                                                                                                       
                  
  `validate()` should accept all structurally valid UUIDs regardless of variant bits, or at least provide a way to validate UUIDs with non-`10x` variants. UUIDs with variant 
  `110x` are produced by real-world systems like AWS Cognito and are valid per the UUID format — they simply indicate a different variant.
                                                                                                                                                                              
  ### Suggested fix

  Change `[89ab]` to `[0-9a-f]` in the validation regex:

  ```diff
  - [89ab][0-9a-f]{3}
  + [0-9a-f]{4}                                                                                                                                                               
  ```
                                                                                                                                                                              
  Or alternatively, expand to `[0-9a-f]` and add a separate `variant()` utility for consumers who need to distinguish variants.

### MRE and Description

# Bug Report: `isValidUuid` rejects valid low-increment UUIDs

## Description
The `isValidUuid` function incorrectly returns `false` for the UUID `00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001`. While this is a "non-random" UUID, it is a syntactically valid 128-bit identifier according to the **RFC 4122** specification.

## Steps to Reproduce
Run the following validation check using the library:

```javascript
import { isValidUuid } from 'uuidjs';

const testUuid = '00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001';
console.log(`Is ${testUuid} valid?`, isValidUuid(testUuid));
items.title: [BUG] 00000000-0000-0000-0000-000000000001 is not treated as valid UUID

items.body:
### Feature description

Windows GUIDs as used in formats such as [ASF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Systems_Format) and [CFBF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Compound_File_Binary_Format), use the similar textual representation as RFC 4122 UUIDs, but with a different binary serialization.

### Binary serialization difference

- **RFC 4122** (canonical / network order)
  All multi-byte fields are encoded big-endian.
- **Windows GUID** binary layout
  The first three fields are encoded little-endian:
  - Data1 (uint32, little-endian)
  - Data2 (uint16, little-endian)
  - Data3 (uint16, little-endian)
  - Data4 (8 bytes, stored as-is)

This difference matters when reading or writing GUIDs from binary formats such as ASF, CFBF, OLE, or COM structures.

### Background

This explains why the identifier `49C1577D-2CB7-41BB-1CF3-08D960A71AAF` appeared valid in #673.
It matches the common Windows GUID textual shape but does not satisfy RFC 4122 variant rules, so rejection by `validate()` is correct from an RFC perspective.

### Proposal: add parser for Windows GUID byte order

The following function mirrors `uuid.parse`, but emits bytes in Windows GUID binary layout. It intentionally does not enforce RFC 4122 version or variant rules.

```js
/**
 * Parse a GUID string into bytes using Windows GUID binary layout:
 * Data1/Data2/Data3 little-endian, Data4 as-is.
 *
 * This is the layout used by ASF, CFBF, OLE, and COM.
 */
export function parseWindowsGuid(uuid: string): Uint8Array {
	// Allow "{...}" common in Windows GUID formatting
	uuid = uuid.startsWith('{') && uuid.endsWith('}')
		? uuid.slice(1, -1)
		: uuid;

	if (!validateWindowsGuidString(uuid)) {
		throw TypeError('Invalid GUID');
	}

	let v;

	return Uint8Array.of(
		// Data1: uint32 little-endian
		(v = parseInt(uuid.slice(0, 8), 16)) & 0xff,
		(v >>> 8) & 0xff,
		(v >>> 16) & 0xff,
		(v >>> 24) & 0xff,

		// Data2: uint16 little-endian
		(v = parseInt(uuid.slice(9, 13), 16)) & 0xff,
		(v >>> 8) & 0xff,

		// Data3: uint16 little-endian
		(v = parseInt(uuid.slice(14, 18), 16)) & 0xff,
		(v >>> 8) & 0xff,

		// Data4: stored as-is
		(v = parseInt(uuid.slice(19, 23), 16)) >>> 8,
		v & 0xff,

		((v = parseInt(uuid.slice(24, 36), 16)) / 0x10000000000) & 0xff,
		(v / 0x100000000) & 0xff,
		(v >>> 24) & 0xff,
		(v >>> 16) & 0xff,
		(v >>> 8) & 0xff,
		v & 0xff
	);
}

/**
 * Validate a GUID string in the common Windows form:
 * 8-4-4-4-12 hex, optionally wrapped in { }.
 *
 * Does not enforce RFC 4122 variant or version rules.
 */
function validateWindowsGuidString(input: string): boolean {
	const s = input.startsWith('{') && input.endsWith('}')
		? input.slice(1, -1)
		: input;

	return /^[0-9a-fA-F]{8}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{4}-[0-9a-fA-F]{12}$/.test(s);
}
```

Would a helper like this, clearly separated from RFC-4122 parsing and validation, be considered in scope for `uuid` as an interoperability utility, or is Windows-specific GUID binary layout considered out of scope for the project?

### Additional information

As I am using this function in 2 different projects:

1. https://github.com/Borewit/music-metadata/blob/master/lib/asf/GUID.ts
2. https://github.com/Borewit/file-type-cfbf/blob/master/lib/guid.ts

I will publish a small package myself, unless you are interested to cover this use case with `uuid`.

### Feature description

Some databases and applications allow users to generate truly random UUIDs that do not adhere to any RFCs. It would be nice to be able to treat any array of 16 bytes as a UUID regardless of whether or not it conforms to a particular UUID version. The unsafe prefix already informs any users that the resulting UUID may not conform to any particular specification.
